reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Haemobilia is bleeding into the biliary tree, most often from an abnormal communication between a vessel and a bile duct
The classic Quincke triad is right upper quadrant pain, jaundice, and gastrointestinal bleeding, although all three features are present in only a minority
Iatrogenic and traumatic causes now predominate, including liver biopsy, percutaneous biliary drainage, cholecystectomy, and blunt hepatic trauma
Other causes include hepatic artery aneurysm or pseudoaneurysm, tumours, gallstones, and vascular malformations
Bleeding may be delayed by days to weeks after the inciting procedure, so a high index of suspicion is needed
Blood clots passing through the ampulla can produce biliary colic and transient obstructive jaundice

Angiographic transcatheter embolisation is the first-line treatment for significant arterial haemobilia, with surgery reserved for embolisation failure and endoscopic therapy used to relieve biliary obstruction
reference.pathophysiology: Haemobilia arises when a communication forms between the hepatic or cystic arterial circulation (less often the portal or venous system) and the biliary tree, allowing blood to enter the ducts and drain into the duodenum. The commonest triggers are hepatobiliary trauma and instrumentation, which can create a pseudoaneurysm or arteriobiliary fistula that ruptures into a duct. Blood in the biliary tract may clot and intermittently obstruct bile flow, producing colicky pain and jaundice, and then decompress into the gut as melaena or haematemesis, giving the characteristic waxing-and-waning presentation.
additionalDifferentials: Upper gastrointestinal bleeding from peptic ulcer or varices
Haemosuccus pancreaticus (bleeding via the pancreatic duct)
Ruptured hepatic tumour into the biliary tree
additionalInvestigations: Cross-sectional contrast-enhanced computed tomography, ideally with arterial-phase angiography, to identify a bleeding source or pseudoaneurysm
Catheter hepatic angiography, which is both diagnostic and therapeutic through embolisation
Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy or side-viewing endoscopy to observe blood issuing from the ampulla of Vater
Liver function tests to characterise the obstructive pattern
Full blood count, coagulation studies, and crossmatch
Abdominal ultrasound to detect ductal clot, dilatation, or an underlying lesion
redFlags: Haemodynamic instability from major arterial bleeding
Delayed severe bleeding after recent hepatobiliary intervention or trauma
Cholangitis or biliary sepsis complicating obstructing clot
reference.prognosis: With modern angiographic embolisation most cases of arterial haemobilia are controlled successfully and the outlook is favourable, although the prognosis worsens with major trauma, underlying malignancy, or delayed recognition.
pitfalls: Not considering haemobilia in obscure gastrointestinal bleeding after a recent hepatobiliary procedure
Attributing biliary colic and jaundice to stones and missing intraductal clot
Overlooking the potentially long delay between the inciting event and the bleed
Proceeding to surgery when transcatheter embolisation would suffice
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Control active arterial bleeding with catheter hepatic angiography and transarterial embolisation, the first-line definitive treatment for most cases
Resuscitate with fluids and blood transfusion and correct any coagulopathy
Relieve biliary obstruction from clot with ERCP, including clot extraction and stenting where jaundice or cholangitis develops
Reserve surgery, such as vessel ligation or hepatic resection, for failure of embolisation or when a surgically correctable lesion or major trauma is present
Investigate and treat the underlying cause, such as a hepatic artery pseudoaneurysm, tumour or gallstone, maintaining a high index of suspicion given delayed presentation after biliary procedures
Monitor for recurrent bleeding, biliary sepsis and haemodynamic deterioration, escalating to interventional radiology or surgery as needed
